title: Scavenger removal: Bird and bat carcass persistence in a tropical wind farm
abstract: Energy produced by wind farms has diverse positive environmental effects, but can also be related to negative impacts, including wildlife mortality through collisions with wind turbines. Bird and bat mortality caused by collisions with wind turbines can be estimated indirectly by counting carcasses within wind farms. However, carcass removal by scavengers often biases such measurements. In this study, we identiﬁed the main scavengers removing bird and bat carcasses in a tropical wind farm. A known fate analysis was done to assess the effect of carcass type (i.e., small bird, large bird, bat), vegetation type (i.e., secondary vegetation, croplands) and season (dry and rainy seasons of 2009) on carcass persistence rates. We identiﬁed three main scavenger groups, with mammals being the most abundant group. Our results show high rates of carcass removal relative to previous studies, especially for bats; there were fewer remaining carcasses after 20 days in our tropical site than in non-tropical environments reported elsewhere. We found a higher carcass persistence rate during the rainy season than in the dry season, possibly due to a greater abundance of food resources for scavenger organisms in the rainy season. Although we found some evidence for higher persistence rates for large bird carcasses than for small bird and bat carcasses during the rainy season, overall carcass type was not a strong predictor of persistence rates. Similarly, we did not ﬁnd a strong effect of vegetation type on carcass persistence rates. Results suggest that in order to estimate accurate bird and bat mortality in tropical wind farm areas, seasonality should be incorporated to correction factors of carcass removal rates.

## 1. Introduction

The establishment of wind farms for energy production is increasing worldwide (Redlinger et al., 2002). Compared to traditional electric power generation, aeolian energy is renewable, does not emit air pollutants, and tends to reduce the use of fossil fuels (Kikuchi, 2008; WWEA, 2010). However, electric power generation by wind farms can have several negative impacts, such as noise, land-use transformation, aesthetic changes, landscape alterations, and wildlife mortality (principally birds and bats) through collisions (Osborn et al., 2000; Johnson et al., 2002, 2004; Barrios and Rodríguez, 2004; Arnett et al., 2008; Baerwald and Barclay, 2009).

Bird and bat mortality caused by wind turbines can be estimated indirectly by counting carcasses within wind farms (Osborn et al., 2000; Smallwood, 2007). Yet, results from such surveys need to be adjusted for: (1) carcass removal, taking into account the time elapsed between the collision and the carcass survey and carcass removal by scavengers, and (2) the efficiency to detect carcasses in the field (Wobeser and Wobeser, 1992; Smallwood, 2007).

Scavenger activity modifies the time that wildlife carcasses remain on site by reducing the number of carcasses that can be recorded in field surveys (Wobeser and Wobeser, 1992). Carcass removal by scavengers depends on the availability and visibility of the carcasses, climate conditions, vegetation type, and the species that comprise the scavenger community (Balcomb, 1986; Linz et al., 1997; Ward et al., 2006; Flint et al., 2010). Additionally, carcass removal by scavengers can be estimated through mathematical functions (Smallwood, 2007; Huso, 2010).

Wildlife carcasses play important ecological roles; they influence some site-specific soil and vegetation conditions and maintain scavenger communities, and thus represent an important energetic component of ecosystems (DeVault et al., 2003). The removal of wildlife carcasses by scavengers has been well studied in temperate and Mediterranean conditions due to the high proportion of wind farms in northern North America and Western Europe (WWEA, 2010). In these areas, carcass removal rates are generally high during the first three to five days after the start of the trials, while carcass persistence has been found to decrease logarithmically (Osborn et al., 2000; Smallwood, 2007; Smallwood et al., 2010). Similar carcass persistence patterns have been found in studies focused on the impact of power lines on birds (Ponce et al., 2010) and in agricultural systems (Rivera-Milán et al., 2004).

Tropical areas have gained importance as generators of wind electric power, though we know of no published studies that report scavenger activity on tropical wind farms. The landscape of our study area has experienced substantial transformation as the result of anthropogenic activities such as agriculture and extensive grazing, and lately due to the rapid establishment of several wind farms, as this area is one of the most productive areas in Mexico and the world for wind-generated electricity. However, the studied wind farm is part of one of the most important bird migration routes in North America (Zalles and Bildstein, 2000). Migrating and resident birds and bats use the mosaic of the different land covers, but the impacts of wind farms on vertebrate flying species are unclear. In this study, we assessed scavenger activity in a tropical wind farm, focusing on: (1) the identification of the species that comprise the scavenger community, (2) the influence of carcass size and type (i.e., small bird, large bird, bat) on carcass removal rates, and (3) the effects of vegetation type on carcass removal rates in disturbed tropical dry forests and croplands during the dry and rainy seasons of one year.

Two main types of vegetation are present within the wind farm area: croplands and tropical forest secondary vegetation resulting from crop abandonment (hereafter referred to as secondary vegetation). There are also areas of riparian forest comprising <1% of the wind farm that were not considered in the study. Croplands have replaced native tropical dry forests, and comprise 67% of the wind farm area.

## 2.2. Scavenger identification

To identify which scavenger species were active within our study site, we placed motion-activated game cameras (Cuddeback, 3.0 megapixels) for image recognition and sand for foot print identification around 10 carcasses per field season.

## 2.3. Scavenger removal trials

## 2. Materials and methods

## 2.1. Study area

This study was undertaken on a wind farm on the Isthmus of Tehuantepec, in southern Mexico (Cervantes-Zamora et al., 1990) (Fig. 1). The climate is tropical sub-humid, with a summer rainfall regime (García, 1988). Annual average rainfall recorded at two meteorological stations near the wind farm is 1019 mm, with highest values in June and September, while the annual average temperature is 25[] C (SMN, 2000). The wind farm has an altitude of 74 masl and covers an area of 982 ha (between 16[] 31[0] 00[00] N, 94[] 52[0] 43[00] W and 16[] 37[0] 08[00] N, 94[] 47[0] 33[00] W) and generates 83.3 MW/h produced by 98 wind turbines Gamesa G-52 (850 kW

Fig. 1. Location of the study area.

We conducted two scavenger removal trials, one during the dry season and another during the rainy season of 2009 (May and September, respectively). We placed bird and bat carcasses in the two main vegetation types (secondary vegetation and croplands). To assess the effect of carcass size and type, we placed bat carcasses collected in situ (i.e., carcasses collected within the wind farm) of the following species to represent themselves: Pteronotus davyii, Pteronotus parnellii, Lasiurus intermedius, Centurio senex, Mormoops megalophylla and Molossus sp. Additionally, we used two size classes of commercial chickens (Gallus gallus): small chickens to mimic small bird carcasses (e.g., passerines), and larger hens to mimic larger birds (e.g., falcons, hawks). We set a total of 60 carcasses per season (20 per carcass type), placed all at the same time for all trials. One carcass was placed per wind turbine randomly selected among the 98 wind turbines. Because the average distance between wind turbines was 130 m, we placed the carcasses within a 50 m radius to ensure independent sampling. The number of carcasses placed in secondary vegetation and croplands corresponded to the proportion of the vegetation types within the wind farm facilities.

The same observer recorded the number of consumed carcasses twice a day (at 07:00 and at 17:00), for 20 days, starting one day after the carcasses were set up. Each carcass was searched for in the place it was deployed, plus in the surrounding 10 m radius. We considered a carcass as removed when: (1) it was not found within the 10 m radius of deployment, (2) only leftovers were left by scavengers (<5% of the body mass), or (3) it was completely covered by termites and/or ants. In the case of partial consumption, the carcass was recorded as removed when most parts of the body (>95%) had been removed.

## 2.4. Data analysis

We estimated carcass persistence rate using a known fate analysis, performed using the program MARK version 6.1 (White and Burnham, 1999). We constructed and tested a set of four a priori models incorporating the effects of time to removal (i.e., survival rates are related in a linear trend over time) and carcass type (divided into three groups: small, large and bat), season (dry season and rainy season), and vegetation type (secondary vegetation and croplands). We did not seek for interactions among co-variables as the objective was to identify the main effects of each co-variable in order to generate more robust, simple models. Model selection was based on the Akaike’s Information Criterion (AIC) adjusted to account for small sample sizes (AICc; Hurvich and Tsai,

1989). Model ranking was based on relative differences of the Akaike Information Criterion (Di) following Burnham and Anderson (2002). The Di values were compared to select the most parsimonious model, and we considered models differing by 2Di from the top model as those that were most supported by our data (Burnham and Anderson, 2002).

## 3. Results

We identified three main scavenger groups: mammals, birds, and arthropods (Table 1). Of them, the gray fox, coyote, and two ant species were the most abundant during the dry season, while the rest of the arthropods were present only during the rainy season. More than 80% of the deployed carcasses were removed between 17:00 h and 7:00 h, indicating the nocturnal habits of scavenger species. Mammals were the most frequent scavenger group identified on sites, followed by birds (Table 1). Although arthropods were found in most of the carcasses, they covered generally small proportions of the carcasses (<10%).

During the dry season, we recorded no carcasses remaining in sites after14 days in croplands or 11 days in secondary vegetation (Fig. 2). Conversely, we recorded remaining carcasses of all types until day 20 in croplands and secondary vegetation during the rainy season, with the exception of bat carcasses in secondary vegetation, which all disappeared between the deploy date and the end of this same day.

“Season” provided the best AIC model for explaining carcass removal rates (DAICc 1⁄4 0.00, AICw 1⁄4 0.96). The estimated seasonal survival rates were 0.0% (SE 1⁄4 0) during the dry season and 21% (SE 1⁄4 5) during the rainy season. The average time to the removal of small carcasses was 4.4 days in the dry season and 2.7 days in the rainy season, while large bird carcasses were removed on average, after 2.1 days and 4.4 days in the dry and rainy seasons, respectively. The average time to the removal of bat carcasses was 2.0 days in both seasons. Survival estimates from the best-fitting model showed that only 9% of carcasses persisted at the end of the whole study period considering both dry and rainy seasons (SE 1⁄4 0.03%). No other model was well supported (all Di > 5), suggesting that carcass type and vegetation type are not important predictors of carcass removal rates (Table 2).

## 4. Discussion

Due to the negative environmental issues that arise from the generation of energy through wind turbines, particularly with

flying species, mortality rates need to be precisely calculated to estimate their real effect (Percival, 2003). However, rates of carcass persistence in the field, which allows correcting mortality estimates related to wind farm facilities, vary in relation to the scavenger community and diverse environmental conditions (Balcomb, 1986; Linz et al., 1997; Ward et al., 2006; Flint et al., 2010). This study reports, for the first time, the nature and identity of the scavenger community in a tropical wind farm facility (Table 1). Due to the habits of the most frequent scavenger visitors, mostly mammals, and the fact that most carcasses were removed between 17:00 and 7:00, our results suggest that most carcasses (>80%) are removed during the night. The latter agrees with previous studies, which report that mammals are the most common scavengers (Kostecke et al., 2001; Ward et al., 2006). It is important to note that we do not have evidence of the identities of all scavenger that removed carcasses, as the presence of these scavengers did not result on the removal of a carcass in all the cases. Thus, we only present data of the identity for the potential scavengers identified on the sites.

Although comparing our results with those from previous studies conducted in non-tropical areas is complicated due to differences in several methodological procedures (e.g., sampling size and effort), we underline some general similarities and dissimilarities. In this study, carcass removal, considering all carcass types, was high (w35% removal in day 1), as outlined by Kostecke et al. (2001), who report that removal rates are considered high when they are between 10 and 50%, after day 1. The latter was not unique to this tropical wind farm, as high removal rates have also been reported for temperate areas (Tobin and Dolbeer, 1990; Arnett et al., 2008; Flint et al., 2010). However, one important difference between our general results and those from wind farms located in non-tropical areas is that the proportion of remaining carcasses after the end of the removal trials (day 20). This proportion of carcasses is lower in our study (w10%) than in previous studies (w30%; Smallwood et al., 2010). In particular, bat carcasses remained on site almost four times less time in our study site than in wind farms from cold and temperate areas (see Arnett et al., 2008 and references therein).

We found that during the rainy season, a higher number of carcasses, particularly small and large birds persisted longer in both croplands and secondary vegetation areas than during the dry season. The lower persistence rate during the dry season suggests greater scavenger activity compared with the rainy season. This could be due to less attractive food resources for scavengers in the rainy season as has been indicated by Flint et al. (2010). Scarcity of

## food resources can also lead scavengers to consume all the available carcasses.

Unexpectedly, we found no support for the models including carcass type as an explanatory variable of carcass persistence. However, we found a pattern indicating a similar proportion of large bird carcasses remaining in both habitats until day 20 during the rainy season (croplands: 50%, secondary vegetation 40%; Fig. 2). These patterns show that large differences in the size of carcasses can, in part, influence carcass removal rates, as recorded in previous studies conducted in both temperate and Mediterranean climates (e.g., Morrison, 2002; Smallwood, 2007; Ponce et al., 2010). This has been attributed to the inability of scavengers to deal with large carcasses (Flint et al., 2010). However, the low carcass persistence during the dry season shows that carcass type does not represent

a determinant characteristic related to their removal, and that the scavengers (e.g., mammals) in the area are able to remove carcasses of any size. Nevertheless, other studies have reported that carcasses represent an important resource for scavengers, specifically facultative ones, during the non-rainy season (Flint et al., 2010), possibly explaining why their persistence is substantially lower than during the rainy season.

Our results reveal that the time elapsed between the deployment of intentionally placed carcasses in a tropical wind farm did not differ between secondary vegetation and cropland. Although previous studies have shown that habitat features (e.g., vegetation cover; Kostecke et al., 2001) affect carcass removal (e.g., Wobeser and Wobeser, 1992; Philibert et al., 1993; Anderson et al., 1999; Morrison, 2002), we found very similar patterns among the studied habitat types. This could have three possible explanations: (1) secondary vegetation patches are arranged in the study area such that they provide ‘natural’ corridors, allowing scavengers from secondary vegetation to remove carcasses from nearby croplands, (2) roads may be facilitating the accessibility of scavengers to the wind farm, or (3) habitat type does not represent a limitation for the distribution of scavengers recorded in our study area. However, these hypotheses remain to be tested.

Carcass removal trials aim to obtain results over a short timeframe, and generally use higher carcass densities than those encountered naturally in a given environment. This can result in saturating the system with carcasses (also known as scavenger swamping; Smallwood, 2007; Smallwood et al., 2010), and can bias persistence rates. However, our results indicated that, in general,

the proportion of carcasses remaining on sites was <25%; thus we consider that the swamping of scavengers in this study did not have a significant influence on carcass persistence rates.

We acknowledge two main limitations of our study. Firstly, we did not use local birds for our treatments, and this has been known to have some influence on carcass removal rates (Bevanger, 1999; Smallwood, 2007; Prosser et al., 2008), in addition to the attractiveness of carcasses for scavengers after a certain period of time (Smallwood, 2007), which remains unknown for tropical areas. Therefore, the use of carcasses of chickens as a surrogate for local birds may be one of the reasons we did not find support for carcass type as an explanatory variable for carcass persistence, as removal rates of these types of carcasses can be higher than those found for local carcasses (Smallwood, 2007). Secondly, our study area is relatively small and does not comprise all possible conditions where wind energy facilities could be established within the tropics. However, our study demonstrates differences in carcass removal rates on wind farms between the tropics and temperate regions. Further studies of carcass removal rates in the tropics are needed to allow the generalization of removal patterns, and to increase our understanding of the way that factors such as season and habitat type influence carcass removal.
